lecture_summary: The lecture develops wave-optics problem solving across double-slit interference, diffraction gratings, spectroscopy, and single-slit diffraction. Its main moves are choosing the correct fringe condition, connecting angle to screen position, deciding between exact trigonometry and a small-angle approximation, enforcing physical order limits, and distinguishing grating bright maxima from single-slit dark minima.

videos.title: Young's Double Slit Experiment
videos.reason: Establishes the prerequisite interference picture, slit–screen geometry, bright-fringe spacing, and constructive versus destructive interference used throughout the lecture.

videos.title: Diffraction Grating Problems - Physics
videos.reason: Directly covers the grating equation and calculations involving fringe order, diffraction angle, wavelength, and line density—the skills needed for the lecture’s lines-per-millimeter and allowable-order examples.

videos.title: Single Slit Diffraction - Physics Problems
videos.reason: Covers single-slit calculations using slit width, wavelength, and screen distance, including the angular and linear width of the central maximum; it reinforces the shift from locating bright grating fringes to analyzing single-slit minima.

coverage_gaps: No strong playlist match covers spectroscopy: wavelength separation, atomic absorption and emission fingerprints, stellar absorption lines, or inferring astronomical composition.
No strong match covers the lecture’s treatment of secondary single-slit maxima, including the midpoint approximation, the sinc-squared intensity law, and the exact condition tan(β)=β.
The playlist descriptions do not confirm coverage of the lecture’s full exact-versus-small-angle comparison or the derivation and symmetric counting of the maximum physically allowed grating orders.
